author: george_avs
content:
I haven't seen any staking protocols use this approach, though it may work in some specific setups

For common LSPs, especially permissionless ones, I think this would be quite complex and require a lot of trust. To simplify, the delegator here is usually a set of smart contracts + committee (oracles) for data that is difficult to obtain onchain. There is no single delegator who can simply keep a secret and hand it over later.

The protocol would need a way to generate and store a key share for each validator, and then pass it to the node operator only after the first deposit is final. Maybe the generation part can be solved with cryptography without adding more trust. But for the second part, someone still has to keep the share and release it at the right time.

So this may work in some setups, but for permissionless delegated staking it mostly moves the problem into trusted offchain key custody

author: kevaundray
content: Does the delegator always need to have the BLS private key or do they just need it to create the initial deposit to register their withdrawal credentials?

author: george_avs
content:
Currently, CL verifies the BLS signature of the first deposit. For top-ups, signature verification is not required.

If the signature is not verified at the time of registration, anyone could front-run any deposits and register their validators under their own WCs.

In practice, delegators do not hold any private keys for validators. Node operators generate private keys on their end and sign a deposit message containing withdrawal credentials that point to the delegate’s address (usually a smart contract). This signed message (https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/blob/master/specs/phase0/beacon-chain.md#depositdata) is then verified by the delegator and can be used for a deposit (with some protection against front-running attacks, of course)
